editorNote: EXTRA EDITION: IBM compatibility is turning a crowded personal-computer boom into an industry standard—and a brutal test of which makers can survive.
morningLine: Big Blue sets the standard, telephone lines promise games and software, and personal computers enter the drafting room.

lead.headline: BIG BLUE SETS THE STANDARD
lead.dek: IBM compatibility redraws the personal-computer map as a booming market enters its first great shakeout.
body: NEW YORK — The personal-computer business has reached the moment when a boom begins to choose its standard. TIME's September 5 survey reports that IBM, only two years after introducing its Personal Computer, has captured 26 percent of unit sales and displaced Apple from first place.

The market remains enormous and unruly: more than 200 American companies now manufacture personal computers, twice the number of two years ago, while 1983 sales are forecast at seven million machines. Yet the center of gravity is unmistakable. About 20 companies already make IBM-compatible systems, and buyers increasingly measure a new machine by the software, dealers, and accessories it shares with Big Blue.

That rush toward compatibility is exposing weak balance sheets. Vector Graphic turned a $2.4 million profit into a $3 million loss and laid off one-quarter of its 400 workers. Victor Technologies lost $11 million in the second quarter and eliminated 350 jobs; Fortune Systems watched an $8 million sales decline turn a $3 million profit into a $3 million loss.

Home-computer makers feel the squeeze as well. TIME says Timex Sinclair 1000 sales fell as much as 50 percent in two months even after its price dropped from $99 to $49.95, while Atari, Texas Instruments, and Mattel absorbed heavy losses. Rumors now point to IBM's own lower-priced home machine, code-named Peanut.

The lesson is no longer merely how to build a clever microcomputer. Compatibility, distribution, production capacity, and the timing of a successor model now decide who can remain in the game. The open frontier is becoming an industry—and IBM has planted its flag at the center.

stories.headline: Games by Telephone Move Closer to Home
stories.dek: Coleco and AT&T propose computer and video-game services delivered over ordinary phone lines.
body: HARTFORD — Coleco Industries and American Telephone and Telegraph announced a joint venture September 8 aimed at bringing home-computer and video-game use over telephone lines. The proposal joins the country's communications network to the fast-growing market for electronic entertainment.

The announcement arrives as Coleco prepares its Adam family computer, an expansion of the ColecoVision platform promoted with 64K of user memory, Digital Data Pack storage, a daisy-wheel printer, and SmartWriter word processing.

Details of the service remain ahead of the hardware, but the ambition is striking: programs and play need not remain sealed inside a cartridge or disk. The telephone may become a road connecting home machines to distant services and other players.

stories.headline: Draft-Aide Puts CAD on the Personal Computer
stories.dek: A five-level drafting line brings specialist design work toward smaller systems.
body: NEW YORK — United Networking Systems introduced its Draft-Aide line September 7 for personal computers as well as larger systems. Five user levels promise to scale computer-aided drafting to different needs.

CAD has long suggested costly specialist equipment. A product family meant to reach personal computers strengthens the microcomputer's case as a practical drawing and design tool, not merely a machine for ledgers, letters, and games.

stories.headline: Young Computer Experts Teach the Teachers
stories.dek: At Stanford, early-teen specialists help nearly 200 educators catch up with a new generation.
body: PALO ALTO — Computer-literate youngsters in their early teens helped instruct educators during a five-week Stanford University training course reported September 11. Nearly 200 teachers and administrators from around the world attended.

The reversal is a vivid sign of the home-computer era. Pupils who learned by exploring machines at home can arrive in class ahead of professional teachers, forcing schools to rethink who holds expertise and how quickly a curriculum can change.
